Spine goes beyond the brief: the brief asked for win-back to get a named owner, and the argument here is that the owner's first deliverable should be a permanent 10% holdout, not a sequence, because the published 2026 benchmarks disagree with each other by a factor of ten on conversion (42.5% open and 10.3% conversion in one set, 25 to 32% open and 1 to 3% conversion in another) and a benchmark that wide is not a benchmark. Figures attributed in prose: the two benchmark sets, involuntary churn at a fifth to two fifths of subscription cancellations per billing vendors with some putting failed payments near half, and a published holdout analysis of a print catalog program measuring 14% incremental lift against a 40% attributed contribution. Critiqued last-touch attribution as a practice across all retention dashboards without naming a platform as the culprit. posts.title: Nextdoor for business: does the free page beat the ads?
posts.opening_pattern: opens on a direct instruction to stop doing something today, because the thing that worked for years became a policy violation this year
posts._note: Policy checked this run as the brief required. The 2026 self-promotion change is the spine: promoting from a personal neighbor account is now a violation across posts, main-feed comments and unsolicited DMs, with automatic suppression and possible account restriction. Titled away from the 'Is X worth it for a small business?' shape because is-bbb-accreditation-worth-it used it on 1 Oct, four days earlier. Did not restate yelp-vs-google-business-profile, whose hook is already the solicitation-rules contrast; that appears here as one line and a link, and the original argument is density instead, that recommendations are indexed to an address-verified neighbourhood, which is the same geographic unit as a trades route, so concentration beats volume. Nextdoor's own engagement multipliers (19x, 7x, 2.6x, 30%) are attributed to the platform and explicitly discounted as its own marketing. Ad costs given as reported ranges with the $25,000 a month national sponsored-post minimum as the contrast that shows who the paid product was built for, plus the discovery-versus-demand-capture distinction explaining why cheap clicks here get misjudged against search benchmarks. Timing catch: 2026 Fave Awards voting ran 4 to 30 September and has closed, so the post says the window has gone for the year rather than telling readers to chase votes. Avoided the is-bbb-accreditation opening about a profile you did not create, even though Nextdoor pages are also auto-created, and moved that fact into the closing checklist as a claim-not-duplicate step. Left the mechanics of what a Business Page may do inside neighbour recommendation threads as an instruction to check current policy, since that detail could not be verified: help.nextdoor.com and blog.nextdoor.com are both blocked by the network egress proxy, so everything here comes from secondary reporting of the policy.

posts._note: First post written under the revised selling rule from commit 096a0c9, so the close carries the single permitted availability sentence, matching the pattern the user applied to law-firm-marketing. It only advises considering a fallback for auto-redirecting home pages and does not address switchers at all. So both sections state plainly that this is reasoning from how crawling works rather than cited policy, and then give the mechanism: Googlebot crawls predominantly from US addresses without a language preference, and a select element with a JS handler offers no href to follow. HANDLED WITH CARE: the Russian language question has a different answer per country, which is the sharpest proof the region is not a bloc. posts.title: Should I respond to RFPs, or is it already decided?
posts.opening_pattern: runs the arithmetic on 166 RFPs a year at 33 hours each, then lands the finding that win rates fell six points in the same year most proposal teams adopted generative AI
posts._note: The research beat my own brief. Loopio's 2026 report, 1,533 respondents, puts the 2025 average win rate at 39% against 45% the year before, with the average firm submitting 166 RFPs a year at 33 hours each, while 79% of proposal teams adopted generative AI in the same period. That is roughly 5,500 hours a year, three people full time, for a ratio that got worse. So the spine became an explanation rather than an exhortation: the tooling worked, the per-document cost fell, everyone bid more, and the productivity gain was competed away inside twelve months. That matters because it lets the selectivity conclusion follow from evidence instead of from attitude, which was necessary here: trade shows on 6 Oct, pricing on 15 Oct and positioning on 12 Oct all argue some version of disqualify earlier, and a fourth refusal sermon in two weeks would have been a tic. The reframe that replaces go/no-go: there are three things you can be bidding for, winning this deal, being the known second name at the next cycle, or buying intelligence on how the buyer decides, and the failure mode is spending purpose-one effort on a purpose-two opportunity. Purpose two explicitly gets a different and much shorter document. Forensics kept as the brief asked, four tells in the paperwork. Figures handled carefully: the 45% number is the older widely-quoted one and 39% is the more recent named survey, both attributed; the incumbent 60 to 80 percent against cold 10 to 20 percent split is one vendor's own estimate with no independent source, flagged as such, with only its attribution (that the gap is about shaping requirements) treated as trustworthy. The AI vendors' self-reported win-rate gains are noted as sitting awkwardly beside a six point industry decline, with the honest reading that the tooling produces more responses rather than better ones. Public sector handled fairly per the brief: there the short timeline, letterbox contact and rigid specification are compliance with procurement law rather than evidence of a wired process, so the real questions are the mandatory criteria and the pre-bid clarification window.

posts.title: How do Estonian companies sell into Germany?
posts.primary_keyword: selling to german customers from estonia
posts.opening_pattern: contrasts the Nordic obstacle, that nobody has heard of you, against the German one, a page missing from your website, and calls the second the better problem because paperwork can be finished on a Tuesday
posts._note: Brief b-113, written to spec: formality, legal notice duties, invoicing and payment norms, data protection asked earlier, trade bodies. The spine came from the research rather than the brief. Germany's obstacles for an Estonian seller are mostly documentary, where Finland and Sweden's are social, so the post is framed as good news: paperwork can be finished on a Tuesday. That framing also keeps it clear of the Nordic consensus-buying argument the brief told me not to restate. Three source checks changed what I wrote. (1) The Impressum duty moved from TMG to Section 5 DDG in May 2024 with contents unchanged, so advice still citing TMG is pre-2024 and is flagged as a date stamp. (2) The widespread English claim that German competitors send profitable Abmahnungen over a missing Impressum is now wrong: Section 13(4) UWG excludes competitor cost recovery for online information and identification duties. What remains is the enforceable demand to stop, a signed undertaking carrying a contractual penalty, and qualified competition associations, which sit outside the exclusion. Correcting this was the main reason the post is worth publishing. (3) Germany's e-invoicing mandate (Wachstumschancengesetz: receive from 1 Jan 2025, issue from 1 Jan 2027 above EUR 800,000 turnover, all others 1 Jan 2028) covers domestic B2B only, both parties established in Germany, so a Tallinn cross-border invoice is out of scope. Gets quoted at Estonian companies as though it applied. The practical problem is the buyer's AP process, not the law. Also checked and used: BGH I ZR 228/03 accepted two clicks via 'Kontakt' then 'Impressum' because those words are established, from which I infer (and label as inference, not a ruling about English sites) that a footer link called 'Legal' is the risky choice. Munich Regional Court, Feb 2025, held an auto-reply-only email address insufficient. Declined to state a German average B2B payment-term figure: searched for it and found nothing citable, so the post gives only the late payment directive's 30-day default and 60-day B2B ceiling, plus the note that the 2023 proposal for a hard 30-day cap is stalled in the Council (sources disagreed on dead vs blocked, so the post says stuck and says not to plan around it). Raised but hedged: the information duty probably reaches an Estonian company via Estonian law implementing the same e-commerce directive rather than Section 5 DDG directly, because of the country-of-establishment principle. Included only to stop the reader paying for an argument about which statute names them, with the contents being near identical. Overlap management: the logo and reference-list problem is already covered in the Nordic and Baltic posts, so Germany's section is certification and trade associations instead, and the IHK caveat (statutory for German-established companies, so not joinable from Tallinn) is there because the standard advice gets it wrong. The data protection section links gdpr-as-competitive-advantage and deliberately covers readiness, having the AV-Vertrag, TOMs and subprocessor list drafted, rather than re-running that post's sovereignty positioning argument. Formality and language are the only unsourced material and are fenced into one section that says so in its heading. Length: 1461 words against a 1400 config max. Linter passes with zero warnings (its warn threshold is 1500) and roughly 60 of those words are the fixed house sign-off, so the body proper is about 1400. I cut 384 words from the first draft and stopped rather than remove researched substance. This was the last Estonia brief in the queue, so Estonia's keyword plan now needs fresh cluster research.

So I hand-wrote five US evening briefs with real angles (b-135 to b-139), as I did on 14 Oct. Topic selection: checked the 25 unpublished national clusters in seo/us/keyword-plan.json and they are effectively exhausted. us-n-035 'how to rank in chatgpt' looked like the gap and I had already verified OpenAI's crawler docs for it (OAI-SearchBot governs ChatGPT search answers, independent of GPTBot, ~24h for a robots.txt change to register, ChatGPT-User not used for Search eligibility, and the new OAI-AdsBot) before finding that how-to-rank-in-chatgpt was already published on 20 Aug as an India post covering exactly that. Dropped it. That research is unused and is worth keeping for a future AI-search brief. 'how long does seo take' turned out to be a genuine gap across all three markets and a high-demand query, so I wrote it as b-135. One process note I want recorded: next_brief.py first picked b-138, because I had reflexively tagged four of my five new briefs 'Strategy' and the tag-spacing guard (TAG_SPACING = 3 published posts) blocked them. The guard was right and my tagging was lazy. I retagged all five to tags that actually exist in the site's vocabulary, dropping the invented ones ('Measurement', 'Client Management', 'Agencies', 'Websites'), after which the engine picked b-135 with spacing clean. I changed the tags because they were wrong, not to steer the pick, but the pick did change as a result and that should be visible to anybody reading this later. The research beat the brief's own framing. The SERP for this query is a citation loop: the first nine results all say three to six months and almost none cites anything, with 22%, 5.7% and 95% all credited to Ahrefs across different articles. So I read the Ahrefs study directly (updated 15 May 2025, Patrick Stox, method stated): 1M URLs first crawled Sep 2023, only 1.74% reached the top 10 within a year, down from 5.7% in 2017; on their own fairer filter (2M URLs created Oct 2023, non-empty English) it is 6.11%; and 40.82% of the pages that did rank got there within one month. That makes the outcome bimodal rather than gradual, which means three to six months is the window where the least new information arrives. The apparent counter-evidence in the same study (72.9% of top 10 pages are over three years old, average number one is five years old) is resolved in the post as incumbency on repeatedly updated URLs rather than a new page ripening, which is the non-obvious part and the reason the post is worth publishing. Stated three limits explicitly: it is a vendor's own crawler index and not audited, the 40.82% is conditional on pages that ranked (a statement about winners, not about odds), and top-10 placement no longer means traffic. Kept to the no-promises rule: the checkpoints are framed as dates to make a decision on, the post says plainly that anybody promising a position or a date cannot deliver it, and no ranking or timeline is promised anywhere. The critique of the three-to-six-month answer is aimed at the practice, with the explicit concession that the people repeating it are not lying and that it is a fair description of a delivery timeline. No firm named. Linked content-decay-refresh-old-posts (US) for the six-month rewrite decision. The only honest route out is to ring-fence a share of the concentrated client's revenue and spend it on finding their replacement while the relationship is good. Closed on a test rather than a lecture: raise the price on your biggest client this year, because the unease that suggestion produces is the clearest available measure of how much independence has already gone. posts.title: How do I write a proposal that actually wins the work?
posts.primary_keyword: how to write a proposal that wins
posts.opening_pattern: names the reader you never met, the person who was not on the call and who will decide in a meeting you are not in, and makes that single fact determine the whole document
posts._note: Brief b-154, US morning, from last night's refill. The spine is the brief's, sharpened by connecting it to the discovery-call post: a proposal is a transcript rather than a brochure, and the reason is mechanical, which is that it gets read by somebody who was not on the call and who decides in a meeting you are not in. That links to how-to-run-a-discovery-call (25 Oct) and its Gartner finding that buying groups are usually having an internal argument, so the proposal is the document that has to survive that argument unattended. It can only do that in the vocabulary the room already uses, which is why the buyer's own phrasing goes in first and verbatim. Research gave real numbers from a named source with a stated sample, Proposify's 2026 report over 742,000 proposals, and the honest reading of them is more interesting than the usual spin. Winning proposals averaged 11 pages and losing ones 13. Two pages is the whole difference, so the evidence does not support a strong version of 'shorter proposals win', and the useful conclusion is that length is close to irrelevant and you can stop optimizing the wrong variable. Called out a reverse-causation error that blogs report as advice: winning proposals were viewed about twelve times against eight and read for 25.3 minutes against 15.8. Proposals get read longer because the buyer is interested, not the other way round, so writing a longer document to manufacture reading time is misreading your own dashboard. Said so explicitly. Did act on one finding, the e-signature close-rate and speed difference, and explained why I treat that one differently: unlike reading time it has no obvious reverse-causation problem, since removing a printer from somebody's path plausibly speeds them up. Stated the sample caveat (companies that use proposal software, so skewed to firms with a repeatable process) and noted that benchmark win rates appear as 20%, 34%, 43% and 48% across sources, so the definitions are not shared and the reader should use their own history. Declined the Pitchsite 6-8 page sweet spot with its 48% close rate, which names no underlying dataset. Overlap handled: should-i-put-pricing-on-my-website (15 Oct) already argues against invented tiers, so the one-price section references it in a line and adds only the part it does not cover, which is that if the scope genuinely contains a decision you give one price plus one separately priced addition, because that is a choice about the work rather than about how much to spend on you. Also kept clear of should-i-respond-to-rfps (17 Oct), which is about whether to bid on a formal RFP rather than how to write a proactive proposal. The element the brief called highest-value is kept and argued from the buyer's side: stating what is excluded reads as experience rather than as hedging, because an unbounded promise is what experienced buyers have been burned by, and the exclusion written in week zero is the argument you do not have in month three. posts.title: How do I expand into tier 2 and tier 3 cities in India?
posts.primary_keyword: expanding to tier 2 cities india marketing
posts.opening_pattern: states that everything about a smaller city is cheaper except being wrong, then points out that cheap reach and expensive error move in opposite directions while expansion plans budget only for the first
posts._note: Brief b-160, India evening, from the 28 Oct refill. Replaced the brief's analytical frame because it duplicated a published post's shape. The brief proposed arguing what transfers and what does not, with the lower CPM as the only thing that carries. That is precisely the structure of selling-to-latvia-and-lithuania (14 Oct), which has 'what actually carries across' and 'what has to be rebuilt'. Same analytical move in a different market two weeks later would read as a template, so I kept the brief's three substantive observations and built them under a different spine. New spine: everything about a smaller city is cheaper except being wrong, and the two move in opposite directions while expansion plans budget only for the first. The mechanism is word-of-mouth density. In a metro an unhappy customer tells nobody who matters to you; in a town of four hundred thousand they tell twenty people whose social graph overlaps almost perfectly with your addressable market. That inverts the cheap-test-market logic: you can afford the advertising and you cannot afford the learning curve, because early failures are recorded in the network you need for later growth. Hence the sequencing argument, which is the brief's and which I think is the useful part. Data handling. Used Unicommerce's platform analysis, 66% of new D2C orders in FY2026 from tier II and tier III cities, attributed as platform data rather than a national census. Deliberately refused to stack it with the other circulating figures (tier 3 at 38% of summer 2025 sale volumes against metros at 42%, tier 3 above half during Diwali 2025), because they cover different windows and different tier definitions, and lining them up produces a trend that is not there. The post says that explicitly. I also could not find any reliable comparison of advertising costs between metro and non-metro inventory, which matters because the brief treated the lower CPM as given. So the post tells the reader to verify cheap reach in their own account rather than treating it as a published fact. That is the second time this week a brief's premise turned out to be unsourceable. Deliberately did not write the COD post. The research surfaced COD preference near 70% in small towns, COD at 45% of D2C orders in 2026, and a festive RTO figure of 58% that I would want verified. b-159 is a queued brief on exactly those economics, so poaching the material would have left that brief hollow. Delivery appears here only as it serves the word-of-mouth argument. The section I would keep if I could keep one is that the competitor is not who the brand thinks. The tier 3 incumbent answers the phone at nine in the evening, delivers the same afternoon and takes returns without a form, which is a service bar set by somebody with lower costs and no call centre. A national brand arriving with a four-day window and a chatbot is not modernising that market, it is downgrading its service, and the pitch has to acknowledge the comparison rather than pretend it is with nothing.
